newsitem.title: USA: Highlights of Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget.

text.p: Here are the highlights of President Bill Clinton's $1.69 trillion budget for fiscal 1998 announced on Thursday. The budget in fiscal 1997 was estimated to total $1.6 trillion. Fiscal year 1998 extends from October 1, 1997 to September 30, 1998.
DEFICIT

The budget aimed for balance by 2002, so the deficit -- currently at $107 billion -- was forecast to reach a $17 billion surplus that year. But the White House said the deficit would edge up to $125.6 billion in the current fiscal 1997 before it turns down again in fiscal 1998 to $120.6 billion and continues falling each year after that.
The deficit projections were based on the assumption that Congress will approve Clinton's budget plan.
ECONOMY

The president's budget predicted continued economic expansion this year. It forecast real gross domestic product to grow 2.0 percent in 1997 and 2.0 precent next year, while inflation as measured by consumer prices would rise 2.6 percent in 1997 and 2.7 percent in 1998.
Unemployment would not change much, coming in at 5.3 percent this year and 5.5 percent next.
TAXES
Clinton's budget proposed $98 billion in tax cuts over five years, targeted at things he wants to promote such as college education and expanded retirement accounts.

Clinton announced in his State of the Union message to Congress Tuesday the tax relief would come through a $500 per child tax credit for low- and middle-income families. This would save taxpayers $46 billion through 2002. His announced $1,500 tax credit or a $10,000 tax deduction for college tuition and training would cost $36 billion.
The White House's proposal to raise the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales to $250,000 per person, or $500,000 per couple, for all Americans would save taxpayers $1.4 billion through 2002.

Clinton also proposed a maximum $5,000 tax credit for companies who give welfare recipients a job, and doubling the income limits on deductible Individual Retirement Accounts to give $5.5 billion back to taxpayers.

The president proposed raising $76 billion in tax revenue over five years. Nearly half of this would come from closing tax loopholes, including a controversial proposal to require investors to use the average price of a stock when figuring gains or losses upon sale. Clinton also proposed to renew the airline ticket tax and other excise taxes.
EDUCATION

Clinton said this is his number one priority for the next four years. His budget proposed $51 billion in the fiscal year starting Oct. 1, a 20 percent increase over current spending. Education spending would rise to nearly $60 billion a year by 2002, even as other programmes are cut.

The money would help set up a programme for national achievement tests in 4th grade reading and 8th grade math, as well as enable 100,000 teachers to be nationally certified as "master teachers." It would expand Head Start to one million children by 2,002, and include $5 billion to help finance new school construction. This includes tax incentives for education.
HEALTH

Clinton proposed $100 billion worth of savings over five years from Medicare, which funds health care for the elderly, and the White House has said this would yield $138 billion in savings over six years.

Savings would chiefly come from health care providers like hospitals, which would lose some $45 billion in payments over the six-year period, as well as managed health care plans, which would lose about $46 billion.

As for Medicaid, the health care programme for the poor, the budget seeks $22 billion in gross savings over five years, which sources have said would be achieved in part by imposing a cap on spending per recipient of the programme.

The budget proposed $18.4 billion over five years to expand health care coverage for children and workers between jobs. It proposed more than $20 billion over five years to restore some welfare benefits and food stamps to the poor, including immigrants, and give business new incentives to hire welfare recipients.
INTEREST ON THE DEBT

The budget foresees the gross national debt rising to $6.7 trillion by 2002 from the estimated $5.5 trillion in fiscal 1997. However, when the amount that the government effectively owes itself is subtracted, the net debt owed to the public and investors when the budget is balanced in 2002 would be $4.3 trillion, up from $3.9 trillion in 1997, and the net interest on the debt owed would be $238.6 billion in 2,002, down from $247.5 billion in 1997.
SPENDING CUTS

Clinton's budget shows spending on domestic discretionary programmes, those whose budgets must be approved every year, would be $58 billion lower through 2002. This assumes Congress adopts Clinton's budget instead of extending current policies unchanged for the next five years.
